name: the golem well
description: Two golems that belong to neither player walk a ring around a stone well in the middle of the board, and every piece that stands in their way is eaten, whoever owns it. The four centre squares are stone: no piece may stand on them or slide through them, though a knight may jump them. The golems circle the twelve squares around the stone, starting on opposite sides of the ring, and each steps one square on after every move. A golem eats any pawn or piece on the square it steps to except a king: a king in its path holds it where it is, and the other golem waits behind. Only a king can take a golem. The ring runs along the third and sixth ranks and the c- and f-files, the very squares pieces develop to, so the middle of the board can only be crossed on a clock. A piece that stops on the ring is safe until a golem comes round, and the pawns of the four central files have to walk into it; the d- and e-pawns then meet the stone and go no further except by capturing. So the game keeps asking when to cross: dash between the golems, go round by the edge files, or march your king out to hold a golem still or kill it, which opens the centre to both armies and leaves your king in the open. Pawns step one square at a time, there is no castling, and the second army is the first turned half a turn, so each king faces the other's queen. Checkmate wins, and so does stripping the other side down to its king, which is how most games between the strongest computer players end. A game that reaches its move limit, or goes a hundred moves without a capture or a promotion, goes to the side with more material.
